title: AI Virtual Try-On for Clothing Photos | AIVideosUGC
description: Show your clothing on a model without booking one. AI virtual try-on turns a flat lay or hanger photo into an on-model shot for your listing.
h1: AI Virtual Try-On for Clothing: Your Garment on a Model
lead: Online shoppers skip garments they can only see flat on a table, but booking a model for every new arrival is hard to afford. Upload one flat lay or hanger photo and AI virtual try-on puts your clothing on a realistic model so shoppers can picture wearing it.
benefits_h2: Why use AI virtual try-on for clothing photos?

benefits.t: Show the garment on a body
benefits.d: Flat lays cannot show where the hem falls or how sleeves sit. The model view answers those questions from one uploaded photo, so buyers can judge the piece before choosing a size.

benefits.t: New arrivals on models the week they land
benefits.d: Each garment gets a person and a believable room without coordinating a shoot. Your new-in collection can show clothes being worn rather than hanging on a rail.

benefits.t: Front and back views on demand
benefits.d: Run a second version from a back source or a clear back description to show collar and rear seams. You give shoppers both sides without asking anyone to pose twice.
The square photo sits beside your existing flat lays on the product page and works in launch posts. Add your real measurements and size chart as text after download.

intro: The example shows a lightweight blue zip jacket over a white tee and stone-colored chinos, with the model standing by a mirror that catches the back of the collar and shoulders. It answers what a flat lay can't: where the hem falls, how the sleeves sit, and how the jacket looks zipped on a body.

For a small clothing shop, it's a way to show a new piece on a person the week it arrives, without booking a model or a studio. These model photos work well on Shopify product pages beside your flat lays.
tip: Hang the garment on a plain wall or spread it out flat, zipped and smoothed, then describe the model and room, such as "man in his twenties, light fitting room."
steps_h2: How to put clothing on a model in 3 simple steps
steps_lead: Three steps turn one garment photo into an on-model view — no casting, no studio, no shoot day.

steps.d: Show collar, closures, pockets, sleeves and hem in one clear view, with stray folds smoothed. A full, even source keeps shape and color reliable.
Describe the model, base layer, pose, light and room, leaving the garment unobstructed. You get a styled view without booking anyone.
Compare the download with the real piece, then add your approved size chart to the listing. The photo is ready for pages and launch posts.

ideas.d: Jackets, overshirts, and cardigans look natural worn open or zipped over a simple base layer.
Pair a front view with a mirror or back view so buyers can judge the cut from more than one side.
Put each new piece on a model the day it lands, so your new-in collection shows clothes on people, not just on hangers.

faq.q: Can my shoppers try clothes on themselves with this?
faq.a: No. This tool is for you as the seller: it turns your garment photo into a model view that you can review and place on your store, launch email or social feed. Shoppers still use your size chart for fit decisions.

faq.q: Can one model appear in every photo?
faq.a: There is no saved model to reuse. The person can look different from one image to the next, so describe age range, hair, build, pose and light consistently when you want a related collection.

faq.q: Does the photo show the true fit?
faq.a: It shows the style and how the fabric drapes, not an exact fit for every body. Publish real garment measurements and a size chart beside the image, and avoid wording that promises a measured result.

faq.q: What garment photo gives the cleanest virtual try-on?
faq.a: Lay the garment flat or hang it straight, show the full outline, smooth non-design folds, and use even light. A clear front view gives the model frame more reliable shape, color, closures and pocket placement.

faq.q: Will the model wear my exact garment?
faq.a: The output is guided by the uploaded garment and keeps its visible shape, color and details on the model. Review buttons, seams, prints and hem against the real item before publishing the photo.

faq.q: Can I see both front and back fit?
faq.a: Yes. Run a front and a back version when construction matters. Use a separate rear source or a clear back description rather than asking a front photo to invent hidden seams or closures.

faq.q: What does a virtual try-on photo cost?
faq.a: Each photo costs 24 credits; a front-and-back pair uses 48 credits. The current total is shown before creation, so you can decide how many views the listing needs. Plan the pair when a collar, back seam or closure matters to the product story.

faq.q: How should I compare the generated view with stock?
faq.a: Keep the approved flat or hanger photo open beside the result. Check the collar, closures, pocket placement, sleeve length, hem and visible color, then publish the model view only when those details still describe the item in stock. Compare the shoulder line and garment length at the same zoom, and retain the source photo beside the model view so a shopper can check both references.

faq.q: Do I still need to hire a fashion model?
faq.a: Not for standard listing and social shots. One uploaded garment becomes an on-model view for a fixed credit cost, so you can cover a full new-in collection without a casting or studio day.

faq.q: Can shoppers mistake the photo for a guaranteed fit?
faq.a: Avoid wording that promises an exact fit. Present the image as a style view, publish real measurements and a size chart beside it, and let shoppers choose their size from those facts.

overview.h2: Show the Garment in a Wearable Context
overview.p: A flat lay tells shoppers what the garment looks like on a table. A model view adds the hem, sleeve, neckline, and overall silhouette in a room that helps them picture the piece in use. Use it as a supporting image beside your clean product shot.

overview.h2: Style the Scene Without Promising a Fit
overview.p: Choose a model, pose, base layer, and setting that fit your collection.

input_guide.h2: Prepare the Garment for a Reliable Try-On

items.d: Photograph the front with collar, pockets, closures, and full hem visible; smooth folds that are not part of the design.
Use a straight or gently angled source rather than a bundle of garments that hides the cut.
Name model age range, pose, base layer, footwear, room, and light without adding a body measurement claim.
If the back matters, supply a rear source or run a separate rear composition rather than asking the front to reveal hidden construction.
Show where a jacket, cardigan, shirt, or dress visually falls on the body.
Place the piece over a simple tee, shirt, or tank so customers can see a complete outfit direction.
Use one room and lighting language for several new arrivals.
Use the downloaded photo on a product page, launch email, or social post after checking the garment.

scene_recipes.h2: Try-On Directions for a Small Collection

items.d: Blue zip jacket over a white tee with hands in pockets, standing beside a fitting-room mirror in soft daylight.
A neutral slip dress on a model near a pale window, with relaxed stance and the full hem visible.
Trousers styled with a tucked knit top and simple shoes on a clean city sidewalk, cropped from head to toe.
Cardigan worn open over a tank in a warm living room, with the sleeve cuff and button placket clear.

after_download.h2: Review the Garment Before It Goes Live

items.d: Check pockets, buttons, zipper direction, collar shape, seams, and hem against the real piece.
Add the approved measurements, model notes, and size chart in your store editor.
Use a full-body frame when hem and proportion matter; use a closer crop when fabric or neckline is the point.

good: Jackets, overshirts, cardigans, dresses, and tops
New arrivals that need a styled scene quickly
Collections that can share one model direction and room
Listings that also provide real size and measurement information
not_ideal: Garments whose construction is hidden in the source
Products where fit or drape needs to be measured or confirmed
Very complex prints where every small motif must align perfectly

visual.overview: Treat a try-on image as a merchandising aid, not a measurement. A clear model frame lets shoppers judge the collar, sleeve length, hem, layering and overall silhouette before they open the size chart. Keep one garment as the subject, describe a pose that leaves its construction visible, and use consistent light and crop across a new-arrivals set. Review the generated frame against the real item, then place the approved image beside measurements, fabric information and care notes on your product page. Record which angle passed review, keep the source and result together, and use the image only where a shopper can still reach the size chart.

steps.prompt: Use the uploaded photo as the product and keep its shape, color and label area exactly. An adult model wears the garment and turns once in soft daylight to show the full silhouette, collar, sleeves, pockets and hem. Keep the pose relaxed and leave enough space for the complete outline. Natural fashion UGC look, eye-level handheld framing, one gentle push-in. Sound: fabric movement, no music. End facing camera with the garment centered for a listing review. Keep the background quiet and leave a clean edge around the garment for a listing crop.
